opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core idea behind what we called budget forcing in the s1 work. The intuition is pretty simple. When a reasoning model is generating its chain of thought, it eventually decides on its own that it's done thinking. It emits the end-of-thinking delimiter and moves on to the answer. But often it stops too early. It hasn't double-checked its work, or it's made a small arithmetic slip it would have caught with a bit more reflection.

So what we do is intercept that. When the model tries to end its thinking, we suppress the end-of-thinking token and instead append something like "Wait." That one word nudges the model to reconsider. Very often it goes back, re-examines a step, and sometimes it catches an error and fixes it. So you're extending the reasoning in a really natural way, without any extra training.

The other side is the budget. If you want to cap compute, you can also force the model to stop. Once it hits a maximum number of thinking tokens, you append the end-of-thinking delimiter, maybe with something like "Final Answer:", and make it commit. So you get a knob in both directions. You can push the model to think longer with "Wait," or cut it off at a hard ceiling.

What I find nice is that this gives you controllable test-time scaling. You can actually plot performance against thinking tokens and see a fairly clean upward trend as you allow more "Waits." We saw that on things like AIME and competition math, using a model fine-tuned on only around a thousand carefully curated reasoning examples. That small dataset plus budget forcing got us surprisingly far.

There are limits, of course. If you append "Wait" too many times, performance eventually flattens. The model can start looping or repeating itself, and the context window becomes a constraint. So it's not infinite scaling. But as a simple, training-free way to trade compute for accuracy at inference time, it worked better than I think a lot of people expected. We also compared it to alternatives, like just telling the model in the prompt to think for a certain length. Those tended to be less controllable. The model doesn't really respect a length instruction very precisely, whereas intervening directly on the decoding gives you much tighter control.

r001.rationale: The response says appending “Wait” often prompts reconsideration and error correction, and describes the approach as improving accuracy at inference time.

r002.rationale: It says that appending “Wait” too many times eventually makes performance flatten, with looping or repetition.

r003.rationale: It describes controllable test-time scaling and a clear upward performance trend as more thinking tokens and “Waits” are allowed, alongside a hard token ceiling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the core of what we called budget forcing in the s1 paper. The basic idea is that once you have a model that's been fine-tuned on reasoning traces, you want some kind of knob at test time where you can dial compute up or down and ideally get better performance the more you spend. And it turns out you can get a surprisingly simple version of that knob with just two interventions on the decoding process.

The first one is a cap. You decide on a maximum number of thinking tokens, and if the model hits that budget, you just forcibly append the end-of-thinking delimiter, maybe something like "Final Answer:", and the model is nudged to stop reasoning and commit to whatever it has so far. That's the lower-compute direction.

The second one, which is the more interesting direction, is extending. When the model tries to end its thinking early, instead of letting it emit the end-of-thinking token, you suppress that and append the string "Wait" to the reasoning trace. And what's nice is that the model then does something that looks a lot like what a person would do if they said "wait" to themselves: it goes back, re-reads what it just did, sometimes catches an arithmetic error or a bad assumption, and then either fixes it or confirms it and moves on. You can do that once, twice, several times, and each time you're spending more test-time compute.

So the way I think about combining them is that the budget defines the envelope and "wait" is how you fill it. You're essentially saying, "I want you to think for at least this long and at most this long," and the "wait" injection is what gets you from the model's natural stopping point up to the minimum you want. And when we plotted accuracy against thinking tokens on things like AIME, we got this fairly clean upward-sloping curve, which is the test-time scaling behavior people are after. That was with only a thousand training examples, so most of the capability was already in the base model and this was really about controlling how it gets deployed.

There are a couple of caveats I'd want to flag. One is that it's not unbounded. If you force "wait" too many times, the model starts going in circles, and you can actually see the accuracy plateau or even dip a little, so there's some sweet spot. The other is that the choice of string matters more than you'd expect. We tried alternatives, "Hmm," "Alternatively," and so on, and "Wait" just happened to work the best for us, but I wouldn't claim there's some deep reason for that beyond the model's training distribution. And compared to things like majority voting or rejection sampling, which scale in parallel, this is sequential scaling, so the later reasoning can actually build on the earlier reasoning, which I think is a big part of why it works as well as it does per token.

r001.rationale: The response describes suppressing the end-of-thinking token and appending “Wait” as a simple way to extend reasoning, with accuracy improving as more thinking tokens are used.

r002.rationale: It says “Wait” worked best among alternatives, but does not state that further variation in the prompting approach yields no additional gains.

r003.rationale: It says the token budget sets the envelope, “Wait” extends reasoning within it, and accuracy showed a clear upward trend as thinking tokens increased.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as two parts of the same mechanism: the token budget determines how much computation you want to spend, and “wait” is a simple way to encourage the model to use more of that budget. If the model tries to finish early, you can suppress that end-of-thinking signal and append “Wait,” which gives it a chance to revisit its reasoning, check an assumption, or try another approach.

That can improve performance, but it’s not simply that more tokens always produce a better answer. The model might repeat itself or reconsider something it already had right. So you want to measure the accuracy-versus-compute tradeoff. You can also enforce an upper limit and tell the model to give its answer when it reaches that limit. Together, those give you a way to control reasoning effort at test time without changing the model’s weights.

r001.rationale: The response says appending “Wait” can encourage more reasoning and may improve performance, but it does not state that simply adding it is generally sufficient to improve performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss varying the “wait” prompting approach or whether variation yields further gains.

r003.rationale: The response describes controlling token use and measuring an accuracy-versus-compute tradeoff, but does not report a clear trend of performance improving as test-time compute increases; it cautions that more tokens do not always help.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two parts of the same mechanism. The token budget controls how much compute you give the model at test time, and “wait” is a simple way to encourage it to use more of that compute. If it tries to finish early, you can append “wait” to its reasoning, which often gets it to check its answer or explore another approach.

But you also need a stopping rule. You can let it continue until a particular budget and then ask it to give its final answer. That gives you a way to study the trade-off between inference cost and accuracy: how much does another chunk of reasoning actually help?

The caveat is that more tokens don’t automatically mean better reasoning. The model can repeat itself or move away from a correct answer. So the interesting thing is whether that additional computation produces useful checking and exploration, rather than just a longer response.

r001.rationale: The response says “wait” can encourage more computation and often prompt checking or exploration, but it does not state that simply adding it is generally sufficient to improve test-time performance.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss varying the “wait” prompting approach or whether such variation yields additional gains.

r003.rationale: The response describes using a token budget to study the cost–accuracy trade-off, but does not claim a clear trend of improving performance as compute increases; it cautions that more tokens do not automatically improve reasoning.
